title: Why India wants a two-year cap on soda ash imports
subtitle: India's trade remedy office has proposed country-wise quotas after Indian makers said imports jumped 89% in 2023-24.
content_html:
Picture a bus with a fixed number of seats. When the seats fill up, nobody else gets on, however long the queue. On 6 November 2026, India's trade remedy office recommended a bus like this for soda ash, a white powder that goes into washing powder, bottles and window panes. For the next two years, only a fixed number of tonnes could come in from abroad.

The office is the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, or DGTR, which works under the commerce ministry. Its plan would let in 7,54,992 tonnes in Year 1 and 7,92,740 tonnes in Year 2, with a separate share for each country, as The Economic Times reported.

What is soda ash, and why should anyone care?

Soda ash is a white chemical powder, also sold as washing soda. Wikipedia lists its everyday uses: it cleans clothes as part of many soap powders, it makes hard water softer, and it is used to make soap, paper and the clear material in bottles and window panes. The Economic Times adds detergents and textiles to the list.

So when soda ash supply changes, the effect can travel far: from a chemical plant in Gujarat to the detergent packet in a kirana shop.

Who asked for the limit, and why?

Five Indian makers asked for it: Tata Chemicals, Nirma, GHCL, DCW and RSPL. They applied through their industry body, the makers' group for alkali producers, according to DGTR's own notice of 16 March 2026, the day the probe began.

The complaint is simple. Foreign soda ash was pouring in. The notice records that imports in April 2023 to March 2024 were 89% higher than a year earlier. Imports' share of all the soda ash India used rose from 13% in 2022-23 to 24% in 2023-24.

Think of a samosa stall in a small lane. One day, a big seller from another town starts selling samosas at a lower price right next door. Your stall still has oil, potatoes and a cook, but customers drift away. That is roughly the story the Indian makers told.

Why did so much soda ash head to India? The makers gave reasons in their application, listed in the DGTR notice. The war between Russia and Ukraine disrupted old trade routes into Europe, so sellers in Turkey and Russia looked for new buyers. Turkey added big new capacity. American makers lost demand in Mexico, a key market for them. The makers said all this spare powder was offered to India at lower and lower prices.

What did DGTR find?

After the probe, DGTR agreed that imports had grown in both real tonnes and in share. As reported by The Economic Times, it said the jump of 89% in 2023-24 had stayed at that level since, and that the rise was "recent, sudden, sharp and significant enough to threaten serious injury" to Indian makers.

The makers had asked for limits for four years. DGTR recommended two.

What is a safeguard, in plain words?

This kind of action is called a safeguard. IASPoint explains it as temporary emergency protection when a sudden rise in imports hurts or threatens the makers at home. Unlike an anti-dumping duty, a safeguard can apply even when the foreign goods are sold fairly.

A safeguard can be a tax on imports or a cap on how much comes in. The soda ash plan is a cap. A tax is like raising the bus fare. A cap is like fixing the number of seats: the fare stays the same, but once the seats are gone, the bus is full.

The World Trade Organization's own page on the soda ash probe by India says a member country may restrict imports this way only for a time, and only if rising imports cause or threaten serious injury.

How would the seats be shared?

Each country gets its own seats. For Year 1, as listed by The Economic Times:

  • USA: 1,59,388 tonnes
  • Turkey: 1,28,697 tonnes
  • Kenya: 1,21,847 tonnes
  • European Union: 1,17,179 tonnes
  • Iran/UAE: 1,10,948 tonnes
  • Russia: 70,289 tonnes
  • China: 46,487 tonnes
  • All other countries together: 157 tonnes

These add up to exactly 7,54,992 tonnes. Year 2 is about 5% bigger, at 7,92,740 tonnes, for a two-year total of 15,47,732 tonnes. Each country's yearly share would be split into four quarterly parts, and no country could go over its share in any quarter.

For an importer, that matters a lot. Under the plan, once a country's seats for a quarter are full, no more soda ash from there can come in until the next quarter.

This 2025 video shows GHCL's managing director talking about Chinese dumping and the solar boom, before this probe began.

Who could feel the pinch?

The buyers of soda ash are the detergent makers, the bottle and window pane makers, and textile and paper firms. A quota does not set a price, and no source has yet put a number on what this plan could do to the price of a detergent packet.

History gives a clue to how buyers react. In an earlier fight over a soda ash safeguard duty, Business Standard reported that the detergent industry, which serves over 200 million households, faced cost pressure from swings in the prices of key ingredients such as soda ash. Groups from the detergent industry and other users argued their side at a public hearing.

This is not the first shield for the makers either. In June 2025, a PTI report carried by The Week said the government extended a minimum import price of Rs 20,108 per tonne on soda ash until 31 December 2025. That rule, first put in place in December 2024, meant foreign soda ash could not come in below that price.

This older ET Now interview with Tata Chemicals' R Mukundan looks at where soda ash prices were heading at the time.

Is the bus already running?

Not yet. DGTR only recommends. IASPoint points out that the recommendation by itself does not impose the limit. The government still has to decide and notify it.

What this means for you

  • If you run a small business that buys soda ash, such as a detergent or soap unit, watch for the government's final notice. It decides how many tonnes can come in each quarter.
  • If you import soda ash, your country's quarterly share is the number to track, not just the yearly total.
  • If you are a student of trade, this is a live example of the difference between a tax on imports and a cap on them.
